notes:
1. Employment Generation — Meaning and Importance

  • Employment generation means creation of productive work opportunities for people who are willing and able to work.
  • Employment provides income, supports household consumption and savings, and improves access to education, health, nutrition, housing and social security.
  • Productive employment is one of the most sustainable ways of reducing poverty and excessive inequality.
📌 Must-Memorise

Employment → Income → Poverty Reduction

2. Employment Policy — Quantity and Quality

  • Economic development requires not only more jobs but also better-quality jobs.
  • Productive employment should ideally provide reasonable income, decent working conditions, skill development and greater employment security.
📌 Must-Memorise

Employment Policy → More Jobs + Better Jobs

3. Working-Age Population — Opportunity and Challenge

  • A large working-age population can support economic growth.
  • However, it also creates a continuous need for sufficient productive employment opportunities.

4. Labour Force — Meaning

  • Labour force includes employed persons plus unemployed persons who are actively seeking and available for work.
📌 Must-Memorise

Labour Force = Employed + Unemployed Job Seekers

5. Workforce — Meaning

  • Workforce includes only persons who are actually employed.
📌 Must-Memorise

Workforce = Employed Persons

6. Labour Force vs Workforce

  • Labour force → Employed + unemployed job seekers.
  • Workforce → Employed persons only.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Labour Force ≠ Workforce

7. Persons Outside the Labour Force

Persons not working and not seeking work can include some:

  • Students.
  • Homemakers.
  • Retired persons.
  • Others not participating in the labour market.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Not Working ≠ Automatically Unemployed

8. Labour Force Participation Rate — LFPR

  • LFPR stands for Labour Force Participation Rate.
  • It measures the proportion of the relevant population participating in the labour market.
📌 Must-Memorise

LFPR = Labour Force ÷ Relevant Population × 100

9. Worker Population Ratio — WPR

  • WPR stands for Worker Population Ratio.
  • It measures the proportion of the relevant population that is actually employed.
📌 Must-Memorise

WPR = Employed Persons ÷ Relevant Population × 100

10. Unemployment Rate

  • The unemployment rate measures unemployed persons as a proportion of the labour force.
📌 Must-Memorise

Unemployment Rate = Unemployed Persons ÷ Labour Force × 100

11. LFPR, WPR and Unemployment Rate — Core Difference

  • LFPR → Labour-market participation.
  • WPR → Actual employment.
  • Unemployment rate → Share of labour force without employment.

12. Low Unemployment Rate — Important Limitation

  • A low unemployment rate does not automatically indicate strong employment conditions.
  • If discouraged workers stop seeking jobs, they may leave the labour force and the unemployment rate can fall without employment rising.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Lower Unemployment Rate ≠ Always More Jobs

13. Main Employment Status Categories

Employment can include:

  • Regular salaried employment.
  • Casual employment.
  • Self-employment.
  • Own-account work.
  • Employer status.
  • Unpaid family work.

14. Regular Salaried Employment

  • Regular salaried employment generally provides wages or salary on a relatively continuous basis.

15. Casual Employment

  • Casual employment usually involves daily, temporary or short-duration work.

16. Self-Employment

  • Self-employment occurs when a person works in an enterprise or activity owned or managed by the person or household.
  • It is a valid form of employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Self-Employment → Employment

17. Own-Account Worker, Employer and Unpaid Family Worker

  • Own-account worker → Operates without regularly employing hired workers.
  • Employer → Operates an enterprise and employs others.
  • Unpaid family worker → Contributes to a household enterprise without receiving a regular wage.

18. Formal Employment

Formal employment generally involves:

  • Recognised employment relationships.
  • Employment records.
  • Defined wages.
  • Greater legal protection.
  • Greater social-security access.

19. Informal Employment

Informal employment often involves:

  • Insecure work arrangements.
  • Irregular income.
  • Limited social protection.
  • Absence of written contracts.

20. Unemployment — Meaning

  • Unemployment occurs when a person willing and able to work cannot obtain suitable employment.

21. Open Unemployment

  • Open unemployment means a willing and available worker has no job.
📌 Must-Memorise

Open Unemployment → No Job

22. Seasonal Unemployment

  • Seasonal unemployment occurs when work is available only during particular periods of the year.
  • It is commonly associated with agriculture because labour demand changes between sowing, cultivation and harvesting periods.
📌 Must-Memorise

Seasonal Unemployment → Work Only in Certain Seasons

23. Disguised Unemployment

  • Disguised unemployment occurs when more workers are engaged than actually required.
  • Some workers can be removed without significantly reducing total output.
  • It is commonly associated with agriculture and family-based activities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Disguised Unemployment → Excess Workers

⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Disguised Unemployment ≠ No Work at All

24. Seasonal vs Disguised Unemployment

  • Seasonal → Employment unavailable during part of the year.
  • Disguised → Too many workers are engaged in the available work.

25. Structural Unemployment

  • Structural unemployment arises when workers' skills or characteristics do not match available jobs.
📌 Must-Memorise

Structural Unemployment → Skill / Job Mismatch

26. Frictional Unemployment

  • Frictional unemployment is temporary unemployment associated with movement between jobs.

27. Cyclical Unemployment

  • Cyclical unemployment arises from downturns in the business cycle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Cyclical Unemployment → Economic Downturn

28. Educated Unemployment

  • Educated unemployment occurs when people with educational qualifications cannot find suitable work.
  • It may arise from skill mismatch, inadequate job creation, geographic mismatch or differences between worker expectations and available jobs.

29. Technological Unemployment

  • Technological unemployment arises when new technology reduces demand for particular forms of labour.

30. Unemployment Types — Memory Chain

  • Open → No job.
  • Seasonal → Part-year work.
  • Disguised → Excess labour.
  • Structural → Skill mismatch.
  • Frictional → Between jobs.
  • Cyclical → Downturn.
  • Educated → Qualified but unemployed.
  • Technological → Technology displacement.

31. Underemployment — Meaning

  • Underemployment occurs when a person has work but available time, skills or productive capacity are not fully utilised.
📌 Must-Memorise

Underemployment → Employed, But Underutilised

32. Time and Skill Underemployment

Time-related:

  • A person wants full-time work but receives only limited hours.

Skill-related:

  • A highly trained worker performs a job that does not use those skills adequately.

33. Underemployment vs Unemployment

  • Underemployment → Has work, but work is inadequate.
  • Unemployment → Has no suitable work despite seeking employment.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Underemployment ≠ Complete Unemployment

34. Education, Employability and Employment

  • Education alone does not guarantee employment.
  • Employment depends on whether education produces relevant skills and whether adequate labour demand exists.
📌 Must-Memorise

Education + Employability + Labour Demand → Employment

35. Employability — Meaning

  • Employability is the ability to obtain, perform and retain productive employment.

36. Structural Transformation — Employment Dimension

  • Structural transformation involves movement of workers from lower-productivity activities towards higher-productivity activities.
  • India needs productive employment growth in manufacturing, construction and services while also raising agricultural productivity.

37. Agriculture — Employment Dependence

  • A large part of India's workforce has historically depended on agriculture.
  • Agriculture's share in output has declined faster than its share in employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Agriculture → Employment Share High Relative to Output

38. Productive Labour Movement

  • Moving workers out of agriculture is beneficial only if they obtain more productive alternative employment.
  • Shifting from low-productivity agriculture into equally low-productivity informal services may create only limited income gains.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Sector Change ≠ Automatically Productivity Gain

39. Employment Elasticity — Meaning

  • Employment elasticity measures how strongly employment changes in response to changes in economic output.
📌 Must-Memorise

Employment Elasticity → Employment Response to Output Growth

40. High and Low Employment Elasticity

High elasticity:

  • Growth creates relatively stronger employment.

Low elasticity:

  • Output can increase without proportionate employment growth.

41. Jobless Growth

  • Jobless growth means significant output growth accompanied by slow or inadequate employment growth.
  • It can occur when growth is concentrated in capital-intensive sectors or productivity rises faster than labour demand.
📌 Must-Memorise

Jobless Growth → GDP ↑ but Jobs Grow Slowly

42. Automation and Employment

  • Automation can reduce labour required for some tasks.
  • At the same time, technological change can create new occupations and industries.
📌 Must-Memorise

Technology → Job Creation + Job Displacement

43. Employment-Rich Growth

  • The development objective is not merely higher GDP.
  • Growth should create sufficient productive employment.
📌 Must-Memorise

Growth + Strong Job Creation → Employment-Rich Growth

44. Agriculture — Rural Employment Base

Rural employment is supported by:

  • Crop cultivation.
  • Livestock.
  • Dairy.
  • Fisheries.
  • Horticulture.
  • Forestry.

45. Allied Activities — Employment Diversification

  • Dairy can provide more regular income than highly seasonal crop work.
  • Fisheries and horticulture create employment in production, processing, transport and marketing.
  • Allied activities can reduce seasonal employment dependence.

46. Rural Diversification

  • Rural diversification means expanding employment beyond crop agriculture.

Rural non-farm work includes:

  • Construction.
  • Small manufacturing.
  • Transport.
  • Retail.
  • Repair services.
  • Tourism.
  • Food processing.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rural Diversification → Reduce Dependence on Crop Agriculture

47. Manufacturing — Employment Engine

  • Manufacturing can absorb workers moving out of agriculture.
  • Labour-intensive manufacturing is particularly important in a labour-abundant economy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Manufacturing → Major Potential Job Engine

48. Labour-Intensive Manufacturing

Important employment-generating activities include:

  • Garments.
  • Textiles.
  • Leather products.
  • Food processing.
  • Furniture.
  • Small manufacturing.

49. Manufacturing — Indirect Employment

Manufacturing also creates employment in:

  • Transport.
  • Logistics.
  • Trade.
  • Repair.
  • Design.
  • Business services.

50. Construction — Employment Role

  • Construction is a major employment-generating sector.
  • Roads, housing, industrial buildings and urban infrastructure generate demand for both skilled and unskilled labour.

51. Construction — Quality Challenges

Construction employment can face:

  • Informality.
  • Limited social security.
  • Occupational-safety risks.

52. MSMEs — Employment Role

  • Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises are important sources of employment.
  • They can often generate jobs with relatively modest capital requirements.
  • MSMEs also support entrepreneurship and regional employment.

53. MSME Employment — Key Requirements

MSME job creation depends on:

  • Formal credit.
  • Technology.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Market access.
  • Skilled labour.

54. Services — Employment Role

  • Services are a major source of both output and employment.
  • Service jobs range from high-skill modern services to lower-productivity traditional activities.

55. Modern Service Employment

Important modern service activities include:

  • Information technology.
  • Finance.
  • Telecommunications.
  • Health care.
  • Education.
  • Professional services.
  • Tourism.
  • Logistics.

56. Traditional Service Employment

Traditional service activities include:

  • Retail trade.
  • Transport.
  • Repair work.
  • Domestic services.
  • Personal services.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Services Employment ≠ Always High-Skill Employment

57. Digital Economy — Employment Opportunities

Digital technologies generate jobs in:

  • Software.
  • Online retail.
  • Digital finance.
  • Data services.
  • Logistics.
  • Platform-based work.

They can also expand remote work and self-employment.

58. Gig Work — Meaning

  • Gig work generally refers to short-term or task-based work.

Examples include:

  • App-based transport.
  • Food delivery.
  • Freelance work.
  • Digital services.

59. Platform Work

  • Platform work uses digital platforms to connect workers with consumers or businesses.

60. Gig Economy — Benefits and Challenges

Benefits:

  • Flexibility.
  • New income opportunities.
  • Easier labour-market entry in some activities.

Challenges:

  • Irregular income.
  • Weak conventional social protection.
  • Employment-status uncertainty.

61. Skill Development — Employment Role

  • Skill development connects workers with changing labour-market requirements.
  • A mismatch between worker skills and employer needs can produce unemployment even when vacancies exist.

62. Important Employability Skills

Important skills include:

  • Technical skills.
  • Digital skills.
  • Communication.
  • Problem-solving.
  • Vocational skills.
  • Entrepreneurial skills.

63. Vocational Education

  • Vocational education provides occupation-specific practical training.
  • It helps connect education more closely with employment requirements.

64. Apprenticeship

  • Apprenticeship combines learning with practical workplace experience.
📌 Must-Memorise

Apprenticeship → Learning + Workplace Experience

65. Reskilling and Upskilling

  • Reskilling → Learning new skills for a different role.
  • Upskilling → Improving existing skills for more advanced work.
📌 Must-Memorise

Reskilling → New Role

Upskilling → Better Skills for Existing Role

66. Technology and Continuous Skill Development

  • Automation, AI and digitalisation continuously alter occupational requirements.
  • Workers increasingly require ongoing reskilling and upskilling.

67. Entrepreneurship — Employment Generation

  • Entrepreneurship creates self-employment and can create jobs for others.
  • Entrepreneurs identify opportunities, organise resources, take risks and create enterprises.

68. Entrepreneurship — Not Only Start-Ups

Entrepreneurship includes:

  • Technology start-ups.
  • Traditional small businesses.
  • Family enterprises.
  • Cooperatives.
  • Self-employed workers.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Entrepreneurship ≠ Technology Start-Ups Only

69. Entrepreneurship — Enabling Conditions

Enterprise development requires:

  • Credit.
  • Business skills.
  • Market access.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Technology.
  • Mentoring.
  • Predictable regulation.

70. Formal Finance — Small Entrepreneurs

  • Formal finance is particularly important for entrepreneurs with limited personal assets or savings.
  • Credit constraints can prevent viable businesses from starting or expanding.

71. Local Entrepreneurship — Employment Effect

  • Small businesses can create jobs close to where people live.
  • This can reduce excessive dependence on migration to major cities.

72. Women's Employment — Major Factors

Women's employment can be influenced by:

  • Education.
  • Social norms.
  • Unpaid household responsibilities.
  • Safety.
  • Transport.
  • Child care.
  • Availability of suitable jobs.

73. Women's Employment — Economic Benefit

  • Greater female employment can raise household income and overall economic output.
  • Education alone may not raise participation if appropriate job opportunities are unavailable.

74. Youth Employment

  • Young people entering the labour market require education, relevant skills, work experience and employment opportunities.
  • Long periods of youth unemployment can reduce future earnings and weaken skill development.

75. Vulnerable Workers — Employment Barriers

Barriers can arise from:

  • Education gaps.
  • Skill gaps.
  • Geography.
  • Discrimination.
  • Disability.
  • Weak social networks.

76. Persons with Disabilities — Employment Inclusion

Employment generation for persons with disabilities requires:

  • Accessible workplaces.
  • Appropriate training.
  • Assistive technology.
  • Equal job opportunities.

77. Inclusive Employment Growth

  • Inclusive employment means wider access to education, training, credit and job opportunities across social and demographic groups.

78. Employment Quality — Meaning

Job quality includes:

  • Earnings.
  • Stability.
  • Safety.
  • Social protection.
  • Opportunities for skill development.

79. Formalisation — Meaning

  • Formalisation brings workers and enterprises more fully into legal, financial, tax and social-security systems.

Potential benefits include:

  • Better institutional credit.
  • Greater worker protection.
  • Better social security.
  • Improved tax compliance.
  • Better economic data.

80. Formalisation — Small-Firm Challenge

  • Formalisation should avoid imposing disproportionate compliance costs on very small enterprises.

81. Social Security

  • Social security protects individuals against economic risks such as:
  • Old age.
  • Disability.
  • Illness.
  • Unemployment.
  • Loss of income.

82. Informal Workers — Social-Security Gap

  • Informal workers frequently have weaker access to conventional employment benefits and social-security protection.

83. Decent Work

  • Decent work combines productive employment with adequate income, workplace rights, social protection and dignity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Decent Work → Productivity + Income + Rights + Protection + Dignity

84. Employment Growth Without Quality

  • A rise in employment numbers alone may not produce strong development outcomes if jobs provide very low wages, insecurity or unsafe working conditions.

85. Major Employment Challenges in India

Important challenges include:

  • Large numbers entering the labour market.
  • Dependence on low-productivity agriculture.
  • Skill mismatch.
  • Large informal workforce.
  • Capital-intensive growth.
  • Automation.
  • Regional imbalance.
  • Migration pressures.
  • Low-paid and insecure work.

86. Capital Intensity — Employment Challenge

  • Capital-intensive production can generate large increases in output without equivalent increases in employment.
  • This can contribute to low employment elasticity and jobless growth.

87. Regional Imbalance and Migration

  • Employment opportunities are unevenly distributed across States and regions.
  • This can encourage migration from areas with fewer opportunities to more dynamic labour markets.

88. Employment Policy — Core Requirements

Sustainable employment generation requires:

  • Economic growth.
  • Labour-intensive production.
  • Relevant skills.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Entrepreneurship.
  • Efficient labour markets.

89. Employment Policy — Multi-Sector Approach

Employment strategy must connect with:

  • Agriculture.
  • Industry.
  • Education.
  • Urbanisation.
  • Infrastructure.
  • Social policy.

90. Employment Generation — Core Development Objective

📌 Must-Memorise

More Jobs

  • Productive Jobs
  • Better Wages
  • Skills
  • Social Protection

91. Labour-Market Indicator Memory Chain

  • Labour Force → Employed + Unemployed Job Seekers.
  • Workforce → Employed only.
  • LFPR → Labour Force / Population.
  • WPR → Employed / Population.
  • Unemployment Rate → Unemployed / Labour Force.

92. Unemployment Memory Chain

  • Open → No job.
  • Seasonal → Part-year.
  • Disguised → Excess workers.
  • Structural → Skill mismatch.
  • Frictional → Between jobs.
  • Cyclical → Downturn.
  • Educated → Qualified but unemployed.
  • Technological → Technology displacement.

93. Structural Transformation Memory Chain

Agriculture Labour Dependence ↓

→ Manufacturing + Construction + Services Employment ↑

→ Productivity ↑

→ Income ↑

94. Employment Elasticity Memory Chain

  • High elasticity → Growth creates more jobs.
  • Low elasticity → Growth creates fewer jobs.
  • Jobless growth → Output rises while employment lags.

95. Rural Employment Memory Chain

Agriculture

  • Dairy
  • Livestock
  • Fisheries
  • Horticulture
  • Rural Non-Farm Work

96. Industrial Employment Memory Chain

Manufacturing

  • Construction
  • MSMEs

→ Major Employment Engines

97. Service Employment Memory Chain

IT

  • Finance
  • Health
  • Education
  • Tourism
  • Logistics
  • Retail
  • Transport

98. Skills and Entrepreneurship Memory Chain

  • Skill Development → Employability.
  • Apprenticeship → Workplace learning.
  • Reskilling → New role.
  • Upskilling → Better existing skills.
  • Credit + Skills + Markets → Enterprise → Jobs.

99. Inclusive Employment Memory Chain

Women

  • Youth
  • Vulnerable Groups
  • Persons with Disabilities

→ Equal Access + Skills + Safety + Opportunity

100. Job Quality Memory Chain

Formalisation

→ Protection

→ Social Security

→ Productivity

→ Decent Work

101. TNPSC Traps

  • Labour force and workforce are different.
  • Labour force includes employed persons and unemployed job seekers.
  • Workforce includes employed persons only.
  • A person outside the labour force is not automatically unemployed.
  • LFPR denominator is the relevant population.
  • WPR denominator is the relevant population.
  • Unemployment-rate denominator is the labour force.
  • A falling unemployment rate does not always mean jobs increased.
  • Self-employment is a form of employment.
  • Open unemployment means no job.
  • Seasonal unemployment means work exists only in certain periods.
  • Disguised unemployment means excess workers are engaged.
  • Disguised unemployment does not mean complete idleness.
  • Structural unemployment means worker-job mismatch.
  • Frictional unemployment occurs between jobs.
  • Cyclical unemployment is linked to downturns.
  • Technological unemployment arises from labour-saving technology.
  • Underemployment is not complete unemployment.
  • Education alone does not guarantee employment.
  • Employability and labour demand also matter.
  • Structural transformation does not merely mean workers leaving agriculture.
  • New employment must be sufficiently productive.
  • Employment elasticity measures job response to output growth.
  • Jobless growth means GDP increases without sufficient job creation.
  • High GDP growth does not automatically guarantee employment-rich growth.
  • Agriculture remains a major employment source.
  • Allied activities reduce seasonal dependence.
  • Manufacturing has strong labour-absorption potential.
  • Construction employs both skilled and unskilled labour.
  • MSMEs support local and regional employment.
  • Services range from high-skill to low-productivity work.
  • Gig work is generally task-based.
  • Platform work is digitally mediated.
  • Gig work can provide flexibility but may lack social protection.
  • Reskilling and upskilling are different.
  • Entrepreneurship is broader than technology start-ups.
  • Self-employment and wage employment are both employment.
  • Women's employment depends on jobs, safety, transport, care responsibilities and social conditions.
  • Formalisation can improve protection and access to institutions.
  • Social security is a major dimension of job quality.
  • Employment must be judged by quantity and quality.
  • Long-term objective → Employment-rich growth.

102. Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Labour Force → Employed + Unemployed.
  • Workforce → Employed Only.
  • LFPR → Labour Force / Population.
  • WPR → Workers / Population.
  • UR → Unemployed / Labour Force.
  • Open → No Job.
  • Seasonal → Part-Year.
  • Disguised → Excess Labour.
  • Structural → Skill Mismatch.
  • Frictional → Between Jobs.
  • Cyclical → Downturn.
  • Underemployment → Work Underused.
  • Employment Elasticity → Jobs Response to Growth.
  • Jobless Growth → GDP ↑, Jobs Weak.
  • Manufacturing → Job Engine.
  • Construction → Job Engine.
  • MSME → Local Jobs.
  • Gig → Task-Based Work.
  • Reskill → New Role.
  • Upskill → Better Current Skills.
  • Entrepreneurship → Self + Other Jobs.
  • Formalisation → Protection.
  • Decent Work → Income + Rights + Security.

103. Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected

  • Employment generation means? → Creation of productive work opportunities.
  • Why is employment important? → Income, poverty reduction, consumption, savings and human development.
  • Labour force means? → Employed + unemployed job seekers.
  • Workforce means? → Employed persons only.
  • LFPR full form? → Labour Force Participation Rate.
  • LFPR formula? → Labour Force ÷ Relevant Population × 100.
  • WPR full form? → Worker Population Ratio.
  • WPR formula? → Employed Persons ÷ Relevant Population × 100.
  • Unemployment rate formula? → Unemployed ÷ Labour Force × 100.
  • Does low unemployment always mean strong employment? → No.
  • Regular salaried employment? → Relatively continuous wage or salary employment.
  • Casual employment? → Temporary or short-duration work.
  • Is self-employment employment? → Yes.
  • Open unemployment? → No job despite seeking work.
  • Seasonal unemployment? → Work available only during some periods.
  • Disguised unemployment? → More workers engaged than required.
  • Main sector associated with disguised unemployment? → Agriculture.
  • Structural unemployment? → Skill/job mismatch.
  • Frictional unemployment? → Temporary unemployment between jobs.
  • Cyclical unemployment? → Unemployment caused by economic downturn.
  • Educated unemployment? → Educated person unable to find suitable work.
  • Technological unemployment? → Job loss due to technological change.
  • Underemployment? → Time or skills not fully utilised.
  • Structural transformation? → Movement towards higher-productivity employment.
  • Employment elasticity? → Responsiveness of employment to output growth.
  • High employment elasticity? → Growth creates more jobs.
  • Jobless growth? → Output rises without adequate employment growth.
  • Main agricultural employment challenge? → High employment dependence with relatively low productivity.
  • Rural diversification? → Expanding livelihoods beyond crop farming.
  • Important allied activities? → Dairy, livestock, fisheries and horticulture.
  • Major rural non-farm jobs? → Construction, manufacturing, transport, trade and services.
  • Why is manufacturing important? → Can absorb labour moving from agriculture.
  • Labour-intensive manufacturing examples? → Garments, textiles, leather, food processing and furniture.
  • Why is construction important? → Large demand for skilled and unskilled workers.
  • MSME full form? → Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises.
  • MSME employment role? → Jobs, entrepreneurship and regional development.
  • Modern service jobs? → IT, finance, telecom, health, education, tourism and logistics.
  • Gig work? → Short-term or task-based work.
  • Platform work? → Work mediated through digital platforms.
  • Main gig-work concern? → Income security and social protection.
  • Employability? → Ability to obtain, perform and retain productive employment.
  • Skill mismatch? → Worker skills do not match employer requirements.
  • Apprenticeship? → Learning combined with workplace experience.
  • Reskilling? → Skills for a different role.
  • Upskilling? → Better skills for an existing or related role.
  • Entrepreneurship contributes through? → Self-employment and job creation.
  • Entrepreneurship limited to start-ups? → No.
  • Major barriers to women's employment? → Safety, transport, household responsibilities, child care, social norms and suitable-job availability.
  • Why is youth unemployment important? → Long unemployment can reduce skills and future earnings.
  • Formalisation? → Bringing workers and firms into legal, financial and social-security systems.
  • Main formalisation benefits? → Credit, worker protection, social security, tax compliance and better data.
  • Social security protects against? → Old age, disability, illness, unemployment and loss of income.
  • Decent work? → Productive employment with income, rights, protection and dignity.
  • Core employment objective? → More Jobs + Better Jobs.
  • Long-term employment strategy? → Growth + Labour-Intensive Production + Skills + Infrastructure + Entrepreneurship + Efficient Labour Markets.
